items.title: Fiscal Policy — Meaning, Objectives & Types
items.body:
## In one line

**Fiscal policy** is how the government uses its taxes and spending to steer the economy — speeding it up in a slump and cooling it in a boom. Asked for its objectives and the expansionary-vs-contractionary distinction.

## What is fiscal policy?

**Fiscal policy** is the use of **government revenue (mainly taxes)** and **expenditure** to influence the economy. It is managed by the **Government (Ministry of Finance)** — distinct from **monetary policy**, which the RBI runs through interest rates and money supply.

**Objectives:** economic growth, price stability, employment generation, balanced regional development, reduction of income inequality and overall economic stability (the classic stabilisation, allocation and redistribution roles).

## Types of fiscal policy

| Type | When used | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Expansionary | Recession/slowdown | ↑ spending, ↓ taxes (e.g., PM Garib Kalyan Yojana, COVID-19) |
| Contractionary | High inflation | ↓ spending, ↑ taxes/duties |
| Counter-cyclical | To smooth the cycle | ↑ spending & ↓ taxes in a slump — *moderates* fluctuations |
| Pro-cyclical | — | ↑ spending & ↓ taxes in a boom — *amplifies* fluctuations |

## Instruments & consolidation

- **Instruments:** taxation (direct + indirect), government spending, public borrowing, deficit financing.
- **Fiscal consolidation:** the government's effort to reduce the fiscal deficit, cut public debt and curb wasteful expenditure.
- **Deficit financing methods:** borrowing from the RBI against issued securities (monetised deficit), market borrowing through bonds and securities, external borrowing, and printing new currency. **Don't confuse:** reducing the **statutory liquidity ratio (SLR)** of banks is a *monetary* tool of the RBI, **not** a method of deficit financing.

## Terms explained

- **Fiscal policy** — the government's use of taxes and spending (run by the Ministry of Finance).
- **Monetary policy** — the RBI's control of interest rates and money supply (a different thing).
- **Counter-cyclical** — acting against the business cycle: in a recession the government should increase expenditure and decrease taxes; in a boom, do the reverse.
- **Deficit financing** — paying for the gap by borrowing or printing money.

## TL;DR

- Fiscal policy = govt revenue + expenditure to steer the economy; run by the Ministry of Finance, not the RBI.
- Objectives: growth, price stability, employment, regional balance, reducing inequality, stability.
- Expansionary policy (↑spend, ↓tax) fights recession; contractionary policy (↓spend, ↑tax) controls inflation.
- Counter-cyclical policy moderates the business cycle; pro-cyclical policy amplifies it.
- Fiscal consolidation = reducing the fiscal deficit and public debt; deficit financing = borrowing/printing money.

items.title: Government Budget — Constitution, Process & Structure
items.body:
## In one line

The **Union Budget** is the government's yearly statement of what it will earn and spend, and the Constitution lays down how Parliament passes it. Asked for Article 112, the six stages and revenue-vs-capital items.

## Constitutional basis

- **Article 112** — the Union Budget is the **Annual Financial Statement (AFS)**, showing estimated receipts and expenditure for the year.
- Prepared by the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance**.
- **2017 changes:** advanced to **1 February**; **Railway Budget merged** with the General Budget; **plan/non-plan** classification **abolished**.

## Six parliamentary stages

1. Presentation of Budget → 2. General Discussion → 3. Scrutiny by Departmental Committees → 4. Voting on Demands for Grants → 5. Passing of the **Appropriation Bill** → 6. Passing of the **Finance Bill** (tax proposals).

## Revenue vs capital budget

| | Receipts | Expenditure |
|---|---|---|
| **Revenue** | Tax + non-tax (no new liability/no asset loss) | Recurring — salaries, interest, subsidies (no asset created) |
| **Capital** | Borrowings, disinvestment, loan recoveries | Creates assets — roads, ports, machinery |

## Government funds

- **Consolidated Fund of India:** all revenues, loans, repayments; withdrawals need parliamentary approval (except charged expenditure).
- **Public Account of India:** provident funds, small savings — government acts as banker; no parliamentary approval for transfers.
- **Contingency Fund of India:** advances for unforeseen expenditure, at the President's disposal; replenished by later approval.

## Types of budgets

**Zero-Based Budgeting** (justify every rupee from zero), **Outcome Budgeting** (track results), **Gender Budgeting** (gender lens), and Balanced / Surplus / Deficit budgets.

## Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)

- **DBT** transfers subsidies and benefits directly into beneficiaries' bank accounts (using Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) to curb leakages and fake beneficiaries in expenditure management. It does **not** change tax devolution to States or the FRBM borrowing limit.

## Terms explained

- **Annual Financial Statement (Article 112)** — the formal name of the Union Budget.
- **Appropriation Bill** — the law that authorises withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund.
- **Finance Bill** — the bill that enacts the year's tax proposals.
- **Capital vs revenue** — capital items change assets/liabilities (roads, borrowing); revenue items are recurring (salaries, interest).

## TL;DR

- Article 112 = Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget); prepared by the Budget Division of DEA, Ministry of Finance.
- 2017 changes: 1 Feb date, Railway Budget merged, plan/non-plan distinction abolished.
- Six stages end with the Appropriation Bill then the Finance Bill.
- Capital receipts create liabilities (borrowing) or reduce assets (disinvestment); revenue receipts do neither.
- Three funds: Consolidated Fund (needs Parliament's nod), Public Account (govt as banker), Contingency Fund (President, unforeseen needs).

items.title: Measures of Deficit & the FRBM Act, 2003
items.body:
## In one line

A **deficit** is the gap when the government spends more than it earns; the **FRBM Act** is the law that caps that gap. Asked for the deficit formulas and the 3%/60% FRBM targets.

## Types of deficit (with formulas)

| Deficit | Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue Deficit | Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts | Operational shortfall / dis-savings |
| Fiscal Deficit | Total Expenditure − (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts) | Total borrowing requirement |
| Primary Deficit | Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments | Borrowing for current expenses |
| Effective Revenue Deficit | Revenue Deficit − Grants for Capital Assets | Revenue deficit net of developmental grants |
| Monetised Deficit | Borrowings from RBI | Deficit financed via money creation |

## FRBM Act, 2003

- **Enacted August 2003** for **inter-generational equity** and long-term macroeconomic stability.
- **Targets:** Central fiscal deficit ≤ **3% of GDP**; States cap deficits at **3% of GSDP**; general government debt ≤ **60% of GDP**, Centre's ≤ 40%.
- **Escape Clause (Section 4(2)):** allows breaching targets for **national security, calamity, agricultural collapse, structural reforms** or a sharp output decline (COVID-19 was treated as a calamity).
- **NK Singh Committee (2016):** reviewed the framework and recommended a **debt-to-GDP anchor** with a fiscal-deficit glide path.

## Terms explained

- **Fiscal deficit** — total spending minus all income except borrowing (the total the government must borrow).
- **Primary deficit** — fiscal deficit minus interest on past debt.
- **Revenue deficit** — day-to-day spending minus day-to-day income.
- **Escape Clause** — the FRBM provision allowing targets to be breached in a crisis.

## TL;DR

- Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − Non-borrowed Receipts = total borrowing requirement.
- Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments.
- Effective Revenue Deficit = Revenue Deficit − Grants for creation of Capital Assets.
- FRBM Act, 2003 caps Centre's fiscal deficit at 3% of GDP and general govt debt at 60% of GDP.
- Escape Clause (Sec 4(2)) permits breaches for calamity/national security/structural reforms.

items.title: Tax Structure — Direct, Indirect & Key Concepts
items.body:
## In one line

**Taxes** are compulsory payments to the government, split into direct (on income) and indirect (on goods/services). Asked for the direct-vs-indirect contrast, which board collects which, and concepts like the Laffer curve.

## Direct vs indirect taxes

| Basis | Direct Tax | Indirect Tax |
|---|---|---|
| Impact & incidence | On the same person | On different persons |
| Burden shift | Cannot be shifted | Shifted to end-consumer |
| Nature | Progressive | Regressive |
| Administered by | **CBDT** | **CBIC** |
| Examples | Income tax, corporate tax | GST, customs duty |

## Direct taxes

- Income Tax & Personal Income Tax (Income Tax Act, 1961), Corporate Tax, **MAT** (on 'zero-tax' companies), Capital Gains Tax, **STT** (2004), Professional Tax (State).
- **Abolished:** **Wealth Tax (2016)**, **Dividend Distribution Tax (2020)**, Banking Cash Transaction Tax (2009).

## Key taxation concepts

- **Tax Buoyancy** = %change in tax revenue ÷ %change in GDP (includes rate changes).
- **Tax Elasticity** = automatic response of revenue to GDP, excluding discretionary rate changes.
- **Tax-to-GDP ratio** — higher ratio means a healthier fiscal position, less reliance on borrowing.
- **Laffer Curve** (Arthur Laffer) — inverted-U: revenue peaks at an optimum tax rate, then falls.
- **Pigovian tax** (A.C. Pigou) — on negative externalities, e.g., carbon tax. **Tobin tax** — on speculative currency transactions.
- **Cess** (tax on tax, earmarked) vs **Surcharge** (tax on tax, general purpose).

## Terms explained

- **Direct tax** — paid directly by the earner; the burden cannot be passed on (income, corporate tax).
- **Indirect tax** — collected via a seller and passed on to the buyer (GST, customs).
- **CBDT / CBIC** — the boards that administer direct / indirect taxes.
- **Cess vs surcharge** — a cess is earmarked for one purpose; a surcharge can be used for anything.

## TL;DR

- Direct taxes (CBDT) are progressive and unshiftable; indirect taxes (CBIC) are regressive and shiftable.
- Abolished direct taxes: Wealth Tax (2016), Dividend Distribution Tax (2020).
- Tax buoyancy = %Δ tax revenue ÷ %Δ GDP; elasticity excludes discretionary rate changes.
- Laffer Curve links tax rate and tax revenue (inverted-U with an optimum rate).
- Pigovian tax targets negative externalities (carbon tax); Tobin tax targets speculative forex trades.

items.title: GST — Framework, Council & GST 2.0 (2025)
items.body:
## In one line

**GST** is India's single nationwide tax on goods and services that replaced dozens of older indirect taxes. Asked for the 101st Amendment, the dual CGST/SGST/IGST design, the GST Council and the 2025 'GST 2.0' rate change.

## GST framework

- Introduced by the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act (2016)**, rolled out **1 July 2017**, on the principle of **'One Nation, One Tax'**.
- A **destination-based single tax**; Parliament and State legislatures have concurrent power.
- **Dual GST:** on an intra-state sale both **CGST** (Centre) and **SGST** (State) are levied; **IGST** is levied by the Centre on inter-state transactions.
- **Outside GST:** petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas, ATF; alcohol for human consumption; electricity.
- Enabling laws (2017): CGST Act, IGST Act, GST (Compensation to States) Act, UTGST Act.

## GST Council (Article 279A)

- Constitutional body; **Chairperson = Union Finance Minister**.
- **Voting:** Centre 1/3rd, all States together 2/3rd; every decision is taken by a majority of not less than **three-fourths (3/4th)** of the weighted votes of members present; **quorum = 1/2** of members.
- GSTN (IT backbone) and the E-Way Bill system (for goods > ₹50,000) support administration.

## GST 2.0 — 2025 rate rationalisation

- Announced **3 September 2025**, effective **22 September 2025**.
- Collapsed six slabs to a simplified structure: **two primary rates of 5% and 18%**, plus a **special 40% rate** on luxury and sin goods (0% retained for essentials). The **12% and 28%** slabs were **eliminated**.
- Rationale: boost consumption amid stagnant wages and cushion the impact of US tariffs; a 'Diwali gift' announced by PM Modi around Independence Day 2025.
- Estimated net revenue impact: ~₹48,000 crore loss (≈₹93,000 cr loss offset by ≈₹45,000 cr from the 40% slab).

## Terms explained

- **GST** — a single destination-based tax on the supply of goods and services.
- **CGST / SGST / IGST** — the Centre's, State's and inter-state components of GST.
- **GST Council (Article 279A)** — the Centre-plus-States body that decides rates.
- **Destination-based** — tax goes to the State where goods are consumed, not produced.
- **GST 2.0** — the 2025 rate rationalisation to 5%, 18% and a 40% special rate.

## TL;DR

- GST: 101st Amendment (2016), rolled out 1 July 2017; destination-based dual tax (CGST+SGST intra-state, IGST inter-state).
- GST Council is a constitutional body under Article 279A, chaired by the Union Finance Minister.
- Council voting: Centre 1/3, States 2/3; decisions need a 3/4th majority; quorum is 1/2.
- GST 2.0 (effective 22 Sep 2025) moved to two primary rates 5% and 18% plus a 40% sin/luxury rate, removing the 12% and 28% slabs.
- GST 2.0 aimed to boost consumption and offset US tariffs; net revenue loss estimated ~₹48,000 crore.

items.title: Union Budget 2026-27 & the Finance Commission
items.body:
## In one line

This note gives the key numbers of the **Union Budget 2026-27** and explains the **Finance Commission** that shares taxes between the Centre and States. Both are high-frequency current-affairs topics.

## Union Budget 2026-27 (presented 1 February 2026)

- Presented by **Nirmala Sitharaman** (equalling P. Chidambaram's record of 9 budgets), under the Third Modi ministry / 18th Lok Sabha.

| Item (2026-27 Budget Estimate) | Figure |
|---|---|
| Total expenditure | ~₹53.5 lakh crore |
| Total revenue | ~₹36.5 lakh crore |
| **Fiscal deficit** | **~4.3% of GDP** |
| Debt | ~55.6% of GDP |

- **New-regime rebate:** no income tax on annual income up to **₹12.75 lakh** (₹12 lakh + ₹75,000 standard deduction).
- Continues the **fiscal-consolidation** glide path (down from 4.9% budgeted in 2024-25) with a high capital-expenditure push on infrastructure.

## Finance Commission (Article 280)

- Constituted by the **President under Article 280**, normally every five years, to recommend **tax devolution** (vertical + horizontal sharing of the divisible pool) and **grants-in-aid** (Article 275) to States.
- The **15th Finance Commission** recommended a **41% vertical devolution** to States.

## 16th Finance Commission

- Constituted **31 December 2023**; **Chairman: Arvind Panagariya** (former Vice-Chairman, NITI Aayog).
- Award period: **1 April 2026 – 31 March 2031** (2026-31); supersedes the 15th FC.
- Task: revenue sharing between the Union and States, and augmenting resources of Panchayats and Municipalities.

## Terms explained

- **Budget Estimate (BE)** — the figures proposed for the coming year.
- **Fiscal deficit (% of GDP)** — the year's borrowing as a share of the economy.
- **Finance Commission (Article 280)** — the body that splits central taxes between the Centre and States.
- **Vertical devolution** — the share of central taxes given to all States together (15th FC: 41%).

## TL;DR

- Union Budget 2026-27 presented 1 Feb 2026 by Nirmala Sitharaman; fiscal deficit target ~4.3% of GDP.
- Total expenditure ~₹53.5 lakh crore; total revenue ~₹36.5 lakh crore; debt ~55.6% of GDP.
- New-regime rebate: no income tax up to ₹12.75 lakh (₹12 lakh + ₹75,000 standard deduction).
- Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280 for tax devolution and grants-in-aid.
- 15th Finance Commission recommended 41% vertical devolution to States.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Public Finance — Budget 2026-27, Deficits & FRBM
items.body:
## In one line

This note covers **Andhra Pradesh's own budget for 2026-27** — its size, deficits and the laws that keep its borrowing in check. Asked as AP-specific public finance.

## AP Budget 2026-27 at a glance

| Item (2026-27 BE) | Figure |
|---|---|
| GSDP (current prices) | ~₹19.75 lakh crore (₹19,75,073 cr), ~12% growth |
| Total expenditure (excluding debt repayment) | estimated ₹3,10,058 crore — about ₹3.10 lakh crore (↑12%) |
| Receipts (excluding borrowings) | estimated ₹2,34,190 crore — about ₹2.34 lakh crore (↑19%) |
| Net borrowing | ~₹75,168 crore |
| Fiscal deficit | 3.8% of GSDP (₹75,868 crore) |
| Revenue deficit | 1.1% of GSDP (₹22,003 crore) |
| Own tax revenue | estimated ~₹1,25,846 crore — roughly ₹1.26 lakh crore (6.4% of GSDP) |

## Fiscal discipline & Finance Commissions

- The **Andhra Pradesh Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2005** sets annual targets to progressively cut the state's outstanding liabilities, revenue deficit and fiscal deficit.
- The **16th (Union) Finance Commission** has recommended an annual fiscal-deficit limit of **3% of GSDP** for states for the **2026-31** period (central capex loans excluded from the ceiling).
- The **State Finance Commission** is constituted by the Governor under **Articles 243-I (panchayats) and 243-Y (municipalities)** to recommend devolution to local bodies.
- AP reported the **highest per-capita expenditure on social-security pensions** among states, as noted by the 16th Finance Commission, driven by the **NTR Bharosa** pension (~₹27,719 crore in 2026-27).

## Terms explained

- **GSDP** — Gross State Domestic Product: the value of all goods and services a State produces in a year.
- **Own tax revenue** — taxes the State itself raises (SGST, excise on liquor, stamp duty, vehicle tax).
- **AP FRBM Act, 2005** — the State law capping AP's deficits and debt.
- **State Finance Commission (Articles 243-I / 243-Y)** — shares State resources with panchayats and municipalities.

## TL;DR

- AP 2026-27 GSDP projected at ~₹19.75 lakh crore (current prices).
- AP 2026-27 fiscal deficit 3.8% of GSDP (₹75,868 cr); revenue deficit 1.1% (₹22,003 cr).
- AP own tax revenue ~₹1.26 lakh crore, 6.4% of GSDP in 2026-27.
- AP FRBM Act 2005 sets annual deficit/debt-reduction targets for the state.
- State Finance Commission: Articles 243-I / 243-Y; Union FC: Article 280.

items.title: Budget Procedure, Articles, Funds & Budget History
items.body:
**In one line:** the Constitution gives every step of the Union Budget its own Article, Parliament passes it through cut motions and the guillotine, and its history has a few famous "firsts".

**Why it is asked:** "which Article deals with vote on account / supplementary grants", "who presented the first budget", interim budget vs vote on account and charged expenditure are standard one-liners.

## The budget Articles

**The story**

| Article | What it provides |
|---|---|
| **110** | Definition of a **Money Bill** (Rajya Sabha can only delay it **14 days**) |
| **112** | **Annual Financial Statement** (the Budget) |
| **113** | **Demands for Grants** — voted only by the **Lok Sabha** |
| **114** | **Appropriation Bill** — authorises withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund |
| **115** | **Supplementary, additional and excess grants** |
| **116** | **Vote on account**, votes of credit and exceptional grants |
| **117** | Special provisions for financial bills |
| **265** | No tax shall be levied or collected **except by authority of law** |
| **266** | **Consolidated Fund of India** and **Public Account of India** |
| **267** | **Contingency Fund of India** |
| **292 / 293** | Borrowing by the Union / by the States — a State that **owes the Centre** needs the **Centre's consent** to borrow (Article 293(3)) |

## Charged vs voted expenditure

- **Charged expenditure** is drawn from the Consolidated Fund **without a vote** of Parliament (it can be discussed). Examples: **emoluments of the President**, salaries of **Supreme Court judges** and the **CAG**, the Speaker and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and **debt charges** of the Government of India.
- Everything else is **voted expenditure**, passed as Demands for Grants.

## Cut motions (to reduce a demand)

| Motion | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Policy cut** | Reduce the demand to **₹1** — disapproval of the policy |
| **Economy cut** | Reduce it by a **specified amount** — to effect economy |
| **Token cut** | Reduce it by **₹100** — to air a specific grievance |

- **Guillotine** — on the last day all remaining demands are put to vote together, whether discussed or not.

## Interim budget vs vote on account

| | Interim Budget | Vote on Account |
|---|---|---|
| Article | Article 112 | **Article 116** |
| Purpose | Financial statement before elections | Money for essential spending until the budget passes |
| Duration | A few months | Usually **two months** — about **one-sixth** of the year's estimate |
| Tax changes | Can propose them | **Cannot** change the tax regime |

## The funds — extra details

- **Contingency Fund of India** — set up under the **Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950**; held by the **Finance Secretary** on behalf of the **President**; its corpus was raised to **₹30,000 crore** in 2021.
- **Public Account** money (provident funds, small savings) belongs to depositors, so it moves **without** Parliament's vote.

## Budget history — firsts

| First | Detail |
|---|---|
| First budget of British India | **James Wilson**, **7 April 1860** |
| First budget of independent India | **R.K. Shanmukham Chetty**, **26 November 1947** |
| Most budgets presented | **Morarji Desai** — **10** |
| First woman to present a budget | **Indira Gandhi** (1970) |
| First full-time woman Finance Minister | **Nirmala Sitharaman**; 'bahi-khata' (2019), paperless budget (2021) |
| Budget time shifted 5 pm → 11 am | **2001** (Yashwant Sinha) |
| Railway Budget merged | **2017** (Arun Jaitley), on the **Bibek Debroy** Committee's advice |

## Budget types — origins in India

- **Zero-Based Budgeting** was developed by **Peter Pyhrr** (1970s) and adopted in India in **1986**.
- **Outcome Budget** began in **2005**; **Gender Budgeting** statement since **2005-06**.
- **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)** began on **1 January 2013**.

## Two UPSC classification questions

- **Capital budget items** (UPSC 2016): acquisition of assets, **loans from foreign governments**, and loans and advances to States and UTs — all three.
- **Non-plan expenditure** (UPSC 2014): defence, interest payments, salaries and pensions, and subsidies — all four (the plan/non-plan split ended in 2017).

**AP link:** Andhra Pradesh's own budget follows the same pattern — its Annual Financial Statement is presented in the AP Legislative Assembly under **Article 202** (the State counterpart of Article 112), and AP draws on its own **Contingency Fund of the State (Article 267(2))**.

**Don't confuse** — *Article 112* (Annual Financial Statement, also covers an interim budget) with *Article 116* (vote on account); *charged* expenditure (not voted) with *voted* expenditure (Demands for Grants).

**Remember it:** "Policy ₹1, Token ₹100, Economy = a set amount."

**TL;DR**
- Article 113 = Demands for Grants (voted only by the Lok Sabha); Article 114 = Appropriation Bill; Article 115 = supplementary, additional and excess grants.
- Article 116 = vote on account (about two months, one-sixth of the estimate; cannot change taxes); interim budget comes under Article 112.
- Article 265: no tax except by authority of law; Article 266 = Consolidated Fund and Public Account; Article 267 = Contingency Fund.
- Article 293(3): a State that owes the Centre needs the Centre's consent to borrow.
- Article 110 defines a Money Bill; the Rajya Sabha can delay it only 14 days.

items.title: Union Budget 2026-27 — The Numbers and the Main Announcements
items.body:
**In one line:** the Budget presented on **1 February 2026** spends about **₹53.5 lakh crore**, keeps the fiscal deficit at **4.3% of GDP**, leaves income-tax slabs unchanged and moves the fiscal anchor from the deficit to **debt (≈50% of GDP by March 2031)**.

**Why it is asked:** the current Budget's headline numbers and two or three named announcements are asked every year; AP gets a direct mention (Rare Earth Corridor).

## Headline numbers (Budget Estimates 2026-27)

**The story**

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Total expenditure | **₹53,47,315 crore** (+7.7% over 2025-26 RE) |
| Receipts other than borrowings | **₹36,51,547 crore** (+7.2%) |
| Fiscal deficit | **4.3% of GDP** (2025-26 RE: **4.4%**) |
| Revenue deficit | **1.5% of GDP** |
| Outstanding liabilities | **55.6% of GDP**; target **about 50% of GDP by March 2031** |
| Public capex | Raised from **₹11.2 lakh crore** to **₹12.2 lakh crore** |
| Interest payments | **26%** of total expenditure and **40%** of revenue receipts |
| Nominal GDP growth assumed | **10%** |

## Direct-tax changes

- **Slabs unchanged**; the new regime still gives **no tax up to ₹12 lakh** (₹12.75 lakh for salaried with the ₹75,000 standard deduction).
- **MAT** rate cut from **15% to 14%**; no new MAT credit from 1 April 2026.
- **STT raised** — futures **0.02% → 0.05%**, options **0.1% → 0.15%**.
- **Share buybacks** taxed as **capital gains** (effective 22% for corporate and 30% for non-corporate promoters).
- **TCS** on remittances above ₹10 lakh for **education or medical treatment** cut from **5% to 2%**.
- **Tax holiday till 2047** for foreign companies offering **global cloud services from Indian data centres**; IFSC tax holiday raised from **10 to 20 years**.
- **Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers — Disclosure Scheme, 2026**.

## Named announcements

| Area | Announcement |
|---|---|
| Banking | **High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat** |
| MSMEs | **SME Growth Fund** of **₹10,000 crore** ('Champion SMEs') |
| Pharma | **Biopharma SHAKTI** — **₹10,000 crore** over five years for biologics and biosimilars |
| Electronics | **ECMS** outlay raised from ₹22,919 crore to **₹40,000 crore**; **Semiconductor Mission 2.0** |
| Climate | **₹20,000 crore** over five years for **carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS)** |
| Minerals | **Rare Earth Corridors** in **Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu** |
| Transport | **Surat–Dankuni** freight corridor; **7 high-speed rail** corridors; **20 new national waterways** |
| Cities | **City Economic Regions** — ₹5,000 crore per CER over five years |

## For comparison — Union Budget 2024-25 (23 July 2024)

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Total expenditure | **₹48.21 lakh crore** |
| Receipts other than borrowings | ₹32.07 lakh crore |
| Fiscal deficit | **4.9% of GDP** (aim: below 4.5% by 2025-26) |
| Capital expenditure | **₹11.11 lakh crore** (**3.4% of GDP**) |
| Tax | Standard deduction **₹50,000 → ₹75,000**; **angel tax abolished** |

**AP link:** the 2026-27 Budget names **Andhra Pradesh** among the four **Rare Earth Corridor** States; AP's own 2026-27 budget (14 February 2026) projects a fiscal deficit of 3.8% of GSDP.

**Don't confuse** — *4.4%* (2025-26 revised fiscal deficit) with *4.3%* (2026-27 target); *₹11.11 lakh crore* (2024-25 capex) with *₹12.2 lakh crore* (2026-27 capex).

**TL;DR**
- Union Budget 2026-27: total expenditure ₹53,47,315 crore; receipts other than borrowings ₹36,51,547 crore.
- Fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP (2025-26 RE 4.4%); revenue deficit 1.5% of GDP.
- Outstanding liabilities 55.6% of GDP; target about 50% of GDP by March 2031 (debt anchor).
- Public capex raised from ₹11.2 lakh crore to ₹12.2 lakh crore; interest is 26% of expenditure and 40% of revenue receipts.

items.title: FRBM in Detail — Rules, Statements, Relaxations and the Deficit Questions
items.body:
**In one line:** the FRBM Act 2003 set deficit and debt targets, its rules and three fiscal statements make the Budget transparent, and the targets have been relaxed in every big shock (2008, 2019, 2020).

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2018 asked the N.K. Singh Committee's debt numbers; UPSC 2025 asked two numerical deficit questions; "most inflationary way to finance a deficit" is a classic.

## FRBM — the details

**The story**

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Enacted | **August 2003**; Rules notified **July 2004** |
| Original aim | Fiscal deficit **3% of GDP**; **eliminate revenue deficit** |
| 2018 amendment | FD **3% by 31 March 2021**; general government debt **60%** and Central debt **40% of GDP by 2024-25** |
| Guarantees | Centre not to give guarantees above **0.5% of GDP** in a year |
| Statements laid with the Budget | **Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement** (three-year rolling targets), **Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement**, **Macro-economic Framework Statement** |
| States | The **12th Finance Commission (C. Rangarajan, 2004)** linked debt relief to States passing their own fiscal responsibility laws — so each State caps its deficit at **3% of GSDP** |

## N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee (2016, report 2017)

- Debt anchor: general government debt **60% of GDP** — **Centre 40%, States 20%** — by **2023** (UPSC 2018).
- Fiscal deficit glide path: **3%** till March 2020, **2.8%** in 2020-21, **2.5% by 2023**.
- A State indebted to the Centre must take the Centre's **consent** before borrowing (Article 293(3)).

## When the targets were relaxed

| Year | Why | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **2008-09** | Global financial crisis — stimulus | Central FD **6.2%** against **2.7%** budgeted; State limit relaxed to **3.5%** (2008-09) and **4%** (2009-10) |
| **2019-20** | **Corporate tax cut** treated as a structural reform (escape clause) | FD revised to **3.8%** from 3.3% |
| **2020-21** | COVID-19 — a national calamity | Escape clause; FD peaked at about 9.2% |
| **2021 onwards** | Glide path | FD below **4.5% by 2025-26** — achieved (4.4% RE) |

## The 16th Finance Commission's fiscal roadmap (2026-31)

- Centre's fiscal deficit down to **3.5% of GDP by 2030-31**; States **3% of GSDP** a year.
- **Off-budget borrowings** to be stopped and brought onto budgets.
- Combined Centre + State debt projected to fall from **77.3%** (2026-27) to **73.1% of GDP** (2030-31).

## Other deficit terms

- **Budget deficit** = total expenditure − total receipts **including** borrowings — no longer used.
- **Crowding out** — heavy government borrowing raises interest rates and squeezes private investment.
- In India deficit financing was used mainly for **economic development** (UPSC 2013); the **most inflationary** way is **creating new money** (UPSC 2011).
- A **decrease in the tax-to-GDP ratio** of a country indicates **slowing economic growth rates** (UPSC 2015) — not necessarily less equitable income distribution.
- Over the decade before 2017 neither the tax-GDP ratio nor the fiscal deficit rose **steadily** (UPSC 2017).
- To cut a persistent deficit: **reduce revenue expenditure** and **rationalise subsidies** — not new welfare schemes or lower import duty (UPSC 2016).

## Worked example (UPSC 2025 pattern)

Revenue expenditure ₹80,000 cr, revenue receipts ₹60,000 cr, borrowings ₹10,000 cr, interest ₹6,000 cr.

1. **Revenue deficit** = 80,000 − 60,000 = **₹20,000 cr**.
2. **Fiscal deficit** = borrowings = **₹10,000 cr**.
3. **Primary deficit** = 10,000 − 6,000 = **₹4,000 cr**.

Second case: FD ₹50,000 cr and interest ₹1,500 cr → **gross primary deficit = 50,000 − 1,500 = ₹48,500 cr** (non-debt capital receipts are already inside FD, so they are not subtracted again).

**AP link:** the **AP FRBM Act, 2005** is Andhra Pradesh's version of the State law the 12th Finance Commission asked for; AP's 2025-26 revised fiscal deficit (4.6% of GSDP) overshot its 4.4% budget estimate.

**Don't confuse** — *2003* (FRBM Act passed) with *2004* (Rules notified, 12th FC); *60/40/20* (debt shares) with *3/2.8/2.5* (deficit glide path).

**TL;DR**
- FRBM Act enacted August 2003; Rules notified July 2004; guarantees capped at 0.5% of GDP a year.
- 2018 amendment: FD 3% by 31 March 2021; general government debt 60% and Central debt 40% of GDP by 2024-25.
- FRBM statements: Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement, Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, Macro-economic Framework Statement.
- The 12th Finance Commission (C. Rangarajan, 2004) linked State debt relief to State fiscal responsibility laws (3% of GSDP).
- N.K. Singh Committee: debt 60% (Centre 40%, States 20%) by 2023; FD 3% → 2.8% (2020-21) → 2.5% by 2023.

items.title: Tax Methods, Reform Committees and Direct Taxes in Detail (incl. Income-tax Act 2025)
items.body:
**In one line:** a tax can be proportional, progressive, regressive or digressive and ad valorem or specific; India's tax system was reshaped by the Chelliah and Kelkar committees, and the **Income-tax Act, 2025** replaced the 1961 Act from **1 April 2026**.

**Why it is asked:** "progressive vs regressive", "ad valorem means", "which committee recommended…", "which tax was abolished in which year" and the new Income-tax Act are frequent one-liners.

## Four basic words

**The story**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Impact** | Who pays the tax **first** (usually the seller/producer) |
| **Incidence** | Who **finally bears** the burden (e.g. the consumer of a sales tax) |
| **Shifting** | Passing the burden from the first payer to someone else |
| **Tax base** | Everything taxed; **broadening the base** raises revenue without raising rates |

## Methods of taxation

| Method | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Proportional (flat)** | Same rate for all incomes | 10% on ₹10,000 and on ₹1,00,000 |
| **Progressive** | Rate **rises** with income | Income tax slabs |
| **Regressive** | Rate **falls** as income rises | Indirect taxes in effect |
| **Digressive** | Rate rises up to a point, then stays constant | Mix of progressive and regressive |
| **Ad valorem** ('according to value') | A **percentage of value** | GST |
| **Specific** | A **fixed amount per unit** | Excise on petrol and liquor |

## Reform committees

| Committee | Key point |
|---|---|
| **L.K. Jha Committee** (1977) | Recommended **MODVAT**, introduced in **1986** — credit for excise paid on inputs |
| **Raja Chelliah Committee** (1991-93) | **Broaden the base**, lower and simpler rates |
| **Vijay Kelkar Committee** (2002) | Abolish **wealth tax** and MAT; simplify direct taxes |
| **Kelkar Task Force** (2003-04) | Implementation of the **FRBM Act** and the first blueprint for **GST** |
| **Swaran Singh Committee** (1976) | Proposed a **duty to pay taxes** as a Fundamental Duty — **not adopted** |

## Direct taxes — the details

| Tax | Point to remember |
|---|---|
| **Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT)** | On 'zero-tax companies'; present form from **1997-98**; rate cut to **14%** in Budget 2026-27 |
| **Alternate Minimum Tax (AMT)** | MAT-like tax on **non-corporate** entities (firms) |
| **Corporate tax cut (September 2019)** | Base rate **22%** for existing companies, **15%** for new manufacturing companies |
| **Capital gains** | Long-term if held beyond the holding period (source text: **36 months**; since July 2024 **12 months** for listed securities, 24 months for others) |
| **Securities Transaction Tax (STT)** | From **2004** |
| **Banking Cash Transaction Tax** | **2005**, withdrawn **2009** |
| **Equalisation levy ('Google tax')** | **6%** on online ads from **2016** — abolished from **1 April 2025** |
| **Professional tax** | Levied by **States** (Article 276), capped at **₹2,500** a year |
| **Wealth tax / DDT** | Abolished **2016** / **2020** |

## New tax regime (default since 2023-24)

| Income (₹ lakh) | 0-4 | 4-8 | 8-12 | 12-16 | 16-20 | 20-24 | Above 24 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rate | Nil | 5% | 10% | 15% | 20% | 25% | 30% |

A rebate makes income up to **₹12 lakh** tax-free (Budget 2025-26); the slabs were left unchanged in 2026-27.

## Income-tax Act, 2025

- Replaced the **Income Tax Act, 1961** (and the failed **Direct Taxes Code Bill, 2010**) from **1 April 2026**.
- Passed August 2025 (assent **21 August 2025**) after a **Select Committee** chaired by **Baijayant Panda**.
- About **536 sections, 23 chapters, 16 schedules** — down from 800-plus sections.
- Replaces 'previous year' and 'assessment year' with one **'tax year'**.

**AP link:** professional tax is a State tax, so Andhra Pradesh collects it itself, while income tax collected in AP goes to the Centre and comes back through devolution (AP's share 4.22% under the 16th FC).

**Don't confuse** — *impact* (first payer) with *incidence* (final bearer); *ad valorem* (% of value) with *specific* (per unit); *MAT* (companies) with *AMT* (non-corporates).

**TL;DR**
- Impact = first payer; incidence = final bearer; shifting = passing the burden; broadening the tax base raises revenue without raising rates.
- Proportional = same rate; progressive = rate rises with income; regressive = rate falls; digressive = rises then stays constant.
- Ad valorem = a percentage of value (GST); specific = fixed amount per unit (excise on petrol).
- L.K. Jha Committee recommended MODVAT (introduced 1986); Raja Chelliah Committee (1991-93) broadened the base.
- Vijay Kelkar Committee (2002) proposed abolishing wealth tax and MAT; Kelkar Task Force (2003-04) gave the FRBM implementation plan and first GST blueprint.

items.title: Indirect Taxes, VAT Principle and International Taxation Terms
items.body:
**In one line:** indirect taxes are collected through sellers, the VAT principle removes 'tax on tax' through input tax credit, and terms like GAAR, DTAA, BEPS and the 15% global minimum tax deal with tax avoidance across borders.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC asked BEPS (2016), VAT as a State subject (2011) and sales tax on toothpaste (2014); avoidance vs evasion and shelter vs haven are common traps.

## Indirect taxes in India

**The story**

| Tax | Point |
|---|---|
| **Excise duty** | Mostly subsumed in GST; still on **liquor** (States) and **petroleum** (Centre) |
| **Customs duty** | Under the **Customs Act, 1962** — Basic Customs Duty, **Countervailing Duty**, **Anti-dumping duty**, export duty |
| **Sales tax / CST** | Subsumed in GST — sales tax was **imposed and collected by the State Government** (UPSC 2014) |
| **Service tax** | From **1994**; subsumed in GST on **1 July 2017** |
| **Entry tax / Octroi** | On goods entering a State / a municipal area |
| **Stamp duty** | **State** tax on property documents |

- **Countervailing duty** offsets an **export subsidy** given by the exporting country; **anti-dumping duty** hits goods sold below their home-market price. Both are imposed on the recommendation of the **DGTR** (Directorate General of Trade Remedies) and are allowed by the **WTO**.

## VAT principle and input tax credit

- Without VAT, each stage pays tax on the full price, including tax already paid — the **cascading effect** ('tax on tax').
- Under **VAT**, each producer gets back the tax paid on inputs — the **Input Tax Credit (ITC)** — so tax falls only on the **value added**.
- VAT was introduced by States from **1 April 2005**; it was a **State subject**, not a Central one (UPSC 2011).

## International taxation terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **GAAR** (General Anti-Avoidance Rule) | In force from **1 April 2017** under the Income Tax Act; strikes down arrangements made mainly to avoid tax |
| **DTAA** (Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement) | Treaty so the same income is not taxed twice — **exemption** or **credit** method; India has DTAAs with **90+** countries |
| **PoEM** (Place of Effective Management) | Decides a company's tax residence by where key decisions are made (from 2017) |
| **BEPS** (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) | MNCs shifting profits to low-tax places; **OECD** project from **2013** — curbs **tax evasion/avoidance by multinationals** (UPSC 2016) |
| **Global minimum tax** | **15%** floor for big MNCs under **Pillar Two** of the OECD/G20 framework |
| **Hawala** | Informal money transfer without moving funds — illegal under **FEMA** and **PMLA** |

## Other tax words

| Pair | Difference |
|---|---|
| **Tax avoidance vs tax evasion** | Avoidance uses **legal** loopholes; evasion is **illegal** concealment |
| **Tax shelter vs tax haven** | Shelter = legal saving **inside** the country; haven = low-tax jurisdiction abroad (**Cayman Islands, Mauritius, Panama, Switzerland**) |
| **Tobin tax** | Tax on short-term currency speculation, after **James Tobin** — also called the **Financial Transaction Tax** or **'Robin Hood tax'** |
| **Robot tax** | Proposed levy on automation that displaces workers |
| **Presumptive tax** | Small businesses pay on a fixed percentage of turnover |
| **TDS** | Tax deducted at source by the payer (e.g. an employer) |

**AP link:** stamp duty and State excise are Andhra Pradesh's own taxes — in AP's 2026-27 budget stamp duty and registration fees are projected to rise 70%, and SGST is the largest own-tax source (36%).

**Don't confuse** — *countervailing duty* (against a foreign subsidy) with *anti-dumping duty* (against below-cost pricing); *avoidance* (legal) with *evasion* (illegal).

**TL;DR**
- Excise still applies to liquor (States) and petroleum (Centre); customs duty is under the Customs Act, 1962.
- Countervailing duty offsets a foreign export subsidy; anti-dumping duty targets below-cost imports; both on DGTR recommendation and WTO-permitted.
- Sales tax was imposed and collected by the State Government (UPSC 2014); service tax (1994) was subsumed in GST.
- VAT avoids the cascading effect through Input Tax Credit; State VAT began 1 April 2005 and VAT was a State subject (UPSC 2011).
- GAAR in force from 1 April 2017; PoEM decides company residence (2017); India has DTAAs with 90+ countries.

items.title: GST in Depth — Constitutional Articles, Committees, Compensation, Composition and GST 2.0
items.body:
**In one line:** GST rests on new Articles **246A, 269A and 279A**, was designed by the Kelkar task force and the Arvind Subramanian committee, ran a five-year compensation scheme for States and was simplified to **5%/18%/40%** by GST 2.0.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2018 asked which items are exempt; UPSC 2017 asked GST's real advantage; the composition limit, GSTN, e-way bill and GST 2.0 dates are current-affairs staples.

## Constitutional base

**The story**

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Bill → Act | **122nd Amendment Bill (2014)** became the **101st Amendment Act, 2016** |
| First State to ratify | **Assam** |
| **Article 246A** | Special power of **Parliament and State legislatures** to make GST laws |
| **Article 269A** | **IGST** on inter-State supplies |
| **Article 279A** | **GST Council** |
| GST Day | **1 July** (GST launched 1 July 2017) |

## Ideas and committees

- First proposed by the **Kelkar Task Force (2003-04)**; announced in the **2006-07 Budget**.
- The **Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers** (chaired by **Asim Dasgupta**) shaped the design.
- The **Arvind Subramanian Committee (2015)** suggested a **revenue-neutral rate of 15-15.5%**.

## GST Council — more details

- Members: Union FM (**Chairperson**), **Minister of State for Revenue**, and the Finance Minister of every State, including **Delhi and Puducherry**.
- A **Vice-Chairperson** is chosen by the State members from among themselves.

## Outside or special under GST

- **Alcohol for human consumption** — outside GST by the Constitution.
- **Five petroleum products** — crude, petrol, diesel, natural gas and ATF — inside the law but taxed only from a date the **Council recommends**.
- **Electricity** — outside. **Lottery, betting and gambling** — **taxable** under GST.
- **Exempt** (UPSC 2018): unbranded **cereal grains hulled**, **chicken eggs cooked**, **newspapers** — but **processed and canned fish is taxed**.
- GST's real advantage is a **single common market replacing multiple taxes** — not cutting the current account deficit or overtaking China (UPSC 2017).

## Compensation, composition and administration

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Compensation to States** | For **5 years** (July 2017–June 2022) for revenue below **14% annual growth**; the compensation cess then repaid back-to-back loans and ended for most goods with **GST 2.0** |
| **Composition scheme** | For turnover up to **₹1.5 crore** (**₹75 lakh** in NE States and Himachal Pradesh); fixed rate on turnover; **no input tax credit** |
| **NAPA** (National Anti-Profiteering Authority) | Under the **CGST Act 2017**; work moved to the **CCI** in **December 2022**; anti-profiteering ended for new cases from **1 April 2025** |
| **GSTN** | Non-profit IT backbone; **100% owned by the Centre and States** |
| **E-way bill** | Needed for goods worth more than **₹50,000** moved beyond **10 km** |
| **GSTAT** | **GST Appellate Tribunal** for GST disputes; principal bench at **New Delhi**, functioning from **2025** |

## GST 2.0 — the steps

1. **15 August 2025** — PM announced next-generation GST reform as a 'Diwali gift'.
2. **3 September 2025** — the **56th GST Council** meeting approved it.
3. **22 September 2025** — new rates took effect ('GST savings festival'): **5%** (merit) and **18%** (standard), **40%** (sin/luxury), **0%** (essentials). The **12% and 28%** slabs were removed.
4. Expected revenue: **₹93,000 crore** lost, **₹45,000 crore** gained from the 40% slab — **net loss about ₹48,000 crore**.

**AP link:** for Andhra Pradesh, **State GST is the largest own-tax source (36% in 2026-27)**; AP, like other States, lost the compensation cushion after June 2022, so GST collections now decide its revenue gap.

**Don't confuse** — *Article 279A* (GST Council) with *Article 269A* (IGST) and *246A* (power to legislate); *alcohol* (constitutionally outside) with *petroleum* (inside, rate not yet notified).

**TL;DR**
- 122nd Amendment Bill (2014) became the 101st Amendment Act (2016); Assam was the first State to ratify; 1 July is GST Day.
- Article 246A = power to make GST laws; Article 269A = IGST; Article 279A = GST Council.
- GST was first proposed by the Kelkar Task Force; the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers was chaired by Asim Dasgupta.
- Arvind Subramanian Committee (2015) suggested a revenue-neutral rate of 15-15.5%.
- GST Council includes the Minister of State for Revenue and State FMs (including Delhi and Puducherry); State members choose a Vice-Chairperson.

items.title: Finance Commissions in Detail — 1st to 16th, the 16th FC Formula and Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
**In one line:** the **16th Finance Commission** (report tabled **1 February 2026**) kept the States' share at **41%**, added a new **'contribution to GDP'** criterion, gave **₹9.47 lakh crore** of grants and raised **Andhra Pradesh's share to 4.22%**.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2015 asked the 14th FC's 42%; the devolution criteria and their weights are classic matching items; AP's share and grants are AP-specific.

## Basics

- **Article 280** — appointed by the **President** every **five years** (or earlier).
- **Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951** — qualifications: a **Chairman** and **four members**.
- **Vertical devolution** = States' share of the **divisible pool**; **horizontal devolution** = how that share is split among States.
- **Divisible pool** = gross central taxes **minus cesses, surcharges and cost of collection**.
- Related Articles: **270** (sharing of central taxes), **275** (statutory grants-in-aid), **282** (discretionary grants).

## The Commissions to remember

**The story**

| FC | Chairman | Point |
|---|---|---|
| 1st (1951) | **K.C. Neogy** | First Commission |
| 12th (2005-10) | **C. Rangarajan** | Debt relief linked to State FRBM laws |
| 13th (2010-15) | **Vijay Kelkar** | GST-linked grants |
| 14th (2015-20) | **Y.V. Reddy** | States' share **32% → 42%** (UPSC 2015) |
| 15th (2021-26) | **N.K. Singh** | **41%** (1% less after J&K became a UT); introduced **demographic performance** |
| **16th (2026-31)** | **Arvind Panagariya** | **41%**; new **contribution to GDP** criterion |

## 16th FC — members

**Arvind Panagariya** (Chairman); **Ajay Narayan Jha**, **Annie George Mathew** and **Manoj Panda** (members); **Soumya Kanti Ghosh** (part-time member); **Ritvik Pandey** (Secretary).

## Devolution criteria — 15th vs 16th FC

| Criterion | 15th FC | 16th FC |
|---|---|---|
| **Income distance** | 45% | **42.5%** |
| **Population (2011)** | 15% | **17.5%** |
| **Demographic performance** | 12.5% | **10%** (now population growth **1971-2011**) |
| **Area** | 15% | **10%** |
| **Forest** | 10% | **10%** (now includes open forest and forest **increase 2015-23**) |
| Tax and fiscal effort | 2.5% | — (dropped) |
| **Contribution to GDP** (new) | — | **10%** |

## Grants (2026-31)

| Grant | Amount |
|---|---|
| **Total grants** | **₹9.47 lakh crore** |
| Local bodies | ₹7.91 lakh crore — rural **₹4.35 lakh crore**, urban **₹3.56 lakh crore**; **80% basic, 20% performance** |
| Disaster management (Centre's share) | **₹1.56 lakh crore** of a **₹2.04 lakh crore** corpus; cost sharing **90:10** (NE and Himalayan) and **75:25** (others) |
| Special infrastructure (urban) | **₹56,100 crore** for wastewater systems in cities of **10-40 lakh** people |
| Urbanisation premium | **₹10,000 crore** (merging peri-urban villages) |

- **Discontinued:** revenue-deficit grants, sector-specific grants and State-specific grants.
- Other advice: review/close **308 inactive State PSUs**; States to privatise **DISCOMs**.

## Andhra Pradesh and the 16th FC

| Item | AP figure |
|---|---|
| Share in central taxes | **4.31%** (14th) → **4.05%** (15th) → **4.22%** (16th) |
| Rural local body grants | **₹16,627 crore** |
| Urban local body grants | **₹12,158 crore** |
| Disaster management grants | **₹6,125 crore** |
| Special infrastructure grant | **Visakhapatnam** and **Vijayawada** — up to **₹5,000 crore each** for wastewater |
| Pensions | AP has the **highest per-capita spending on social security pensions** (**₹5,061** per person); a check found **9%** of beneficiaries ineligible |

**Don't confuse** — *41%* (15th and 16th FC) with *42%* (14th FC) and *32%* (13th FC level that the 14th raised); *Y.V. Reddy* (14th) with *N.K. Singh* (15th and the FRBM review).

**TL;DR**
- Finance Commission: Article 280, every five years; FC (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1951 — Chairman plus four members.
- Divisible pool excludes cesses, surcharges and cost of collection; vertical = States' share, horizontal = split among States.
- Article 270 (sharing of central taxes), Article 275 (statutory grants-in-aid), Article 282 (discretionary grants).
- 1st FC K.C. Neogy; 12th C. Rangarajan; 13th Vijay Kelkar; 14th Y.V. Reddy (32% → 42%); 15th N.K. Singh (41%).
- 16th FC members: Ajay Narayan Jha, Annie George Mathew, Manoj Panda; Soumya Kanti Ghosh part-time; Ritvik Pandey Secretary.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Budget 2026-27 — Receipts, Spending, Debt and Schemes
items.body:
**In one line:** AP Finance Minister **Payyavula Keshav** presented the 2026-27 Budget on **14 February 2026** — revenue receipts of **₹2.34 lakh crore** (59% the State's own), capital outlay up **47%**, and outstanding liabilities steady at **36% of GSDP**.

**Why it is asked:** AP's own budget numbers, its largest tax source, its debt and off-budget borrowing are standard AP-specific questions.

## Receipts

**The story**

| Item (2026-27 BE) | Figure |
|---|---|
| Revenue receipts | **₹2,34,140 crore** (+19%) |
| From the State's own resources | **₹1,37,320 crore — 59%** |
| From the Centre | **₹96,820 crore — 41%** |
| Share in central taxes | **₹64,362 crore** (27% of revenue receipts) |
| Grants from the Centre | **₹32,458 crore** (14%) |
| Largest own-tax source | **State GST — 36%** of own tax revenue |
| Stamp duty and registration | Projected **+70%** |
| Non-tax revenue from mining | ₹5,196 crore (only **16%** of auctioned blocks operational, Jan 2025) |

## Spending

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Revenue expenditure | **₹2,56,143 crore** (+8%) |
| **Capital outlay** | **₹48,698 crore** (**+47%**) — irrigation, water supply, urban development |
| Interest payments | **₹37,281 crore** (16% of revenue receipts) |
| Pensions | **₹23,713 crore** (10% of revenue receipts) |
| Debt repaid | **₹22,147 crore** |
| NTR Bharosa pensions | **₹27,719 crore** |
| Stree Shakti (free bus travel for women) | **₹1,420 crore** |
| Dr NTR Vaidya Seva Trust | **₹4,000 crore** |

- Share of spending: **education 11.7%** (States' average 14.5%), **health 6.4%**, **rural development 6.8%**, agriculture 4.7%, **roads 0.9%** (average 4.3%).

## Deficits and debt

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| 2025-26 revised fiscal deficit | **4.6% of GSDP** (budgeted 4.4%) |
| 2025-26 revised revenue deficit | **2.3% of GSDP** (budgeted 1.8%) |
| Outstanding liabilities | **36% of GSDP** (33% in 2021-22) |
| Outstanding guarantees | **₹1,77,328 crore** (10% of GSDP, Dec 2025) |
| Off-budget borrowings (CAG 2024) | **₹1.28 lakh crore** (9.7% of GSDP, March 2023) |
| Central 50-year capex loans | ₹11,000 crore — **outside** the borrowing ceiling |

## AP economy snapshot (2024-25)

- Real GSDP growth **8%** vs India **6.5%**.
- Sector shares (current prices): **agriculture 37%**, industry 21%, **services 42%**.
- **Per-capita GSDP ₹2,98,058** vs India's per-capita GDP ₹2,34,859.

## Policy announcements

- **Free power for weavers** from 1 April 2026 — **200 units** (handloom) and **500 units** (power loom) a month.
- **Andhra Pradesh Wealth Fund** — a **sovereign wealth fund** for the State's assets.
- **Harita Andhra Pradesh** — green cover from **30%** (2026) to **37% by 2030** and **50% by 2047**.
- Police: **3,000** new vehicles and a **cybercrime police station in every district**.

**Don't confuse** — *revenue receipts ₹2.34 lakh crore* with *expenditure ₹3.10 lakh crore*; *59% own resources* with *41% from the Centre*; *36%* (outstanding liabilities) with *36%* (SGST share of own taxes).

**TL;DR**
- AP Budget 2026-27 was presented by Finance Minister Payyavula Keshav on 14 February 2026.
- AP revenue receipts ₹2,34,140 crore: 59% own resources (₹1,37,320 crore), 41% from the Centre (₹96,820 crore).
- AP share in central taxes ₹64,362 crore and grants ₹32,458 crore in 2026-27.
- State GST is AP's largest own-tax source (36%); stamp duty and registration are projected to rise 70%.
- AP capital outlay ₹48,698 crore (+47%); revenue expenditure ₹2,56,143 crore; interest ₹37,281 crore; pensions ₹23,713 crore.

items.title: For Mains — Fiscal Policy, Budget & GST
items.body:
## In one line

For Mains, this topic is a debate on **resource mobilisation and fiscal discipline**: can the government fund development, keep deficits in check, and run GST as true cooperative federalism? (Serves mains-3 clause M3-15e on Tax Laws and mains-4 clauses M4-2 and M4-4.)

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Features | FRBM targets, budget structure, dual-GST design, GST Council (Article 279A) |
| Significance | Rules-based discipline, One-Nation-One-Tax, pooled sovereignty |
| Impact | Consolidation glide path (FD 4.3% in 2026-27), simpler GST 2.0, higher capex |
| Criticism / limits | Revenue loss from GST 2.0, exclusion of petroleum/alcohol, States' revenue stress |
| Way forward | Buoyant collections, widen GST base, predictable devolution, debt-to-GDP anchor |

## Data / committees / reports to quote

- **FRBM Act, 2003** — FD ≤3% of GDP, debt ≤60%; **NK Singh Committee (2016)** debt-anchor glide path.
- **Union Budget 2026-27:** expenditure ≈₹53.5 lakh crore, receipts ≈₹36.5 lakh crore, **FD 4.3% of GDP**, rebate up to ₹12.75 lakh (PRS, 1 Feb 2026).
- **GST 2.0 (22 Sep 2025):** slabs cut to **5%, 18% and 40%**; net revenue loss ≈₹48,000 crore.
- **16th Finance Commission** (Panagariya, 2026-31); 15th FC devolution 41%.

## AP angle

**Andhra Pradesh** has run **revenue deficits since bifurcation**; the end of the GST compensation cess and a 3%-of-GSDP ceiling make predictable **16th FC transfers** critical. AP's 2026-27 FD is 3.8% of GSDP.

## Use in answers

- **Example:** cite GST 2.0's 5/18/40 structure as a consumption-boosting, federalism-testing reform.
- **Quote:** the GST Council is India's finest experiment in **'pooled sovereignty'**.
- **Diagram idea:** a flow of the divisible pool from the Centre to States and local bodies.
keyPoints: Mains frames this as resource mobilisation + fiscal discipline + cooperative federalism (M3-15e, M4-2, M4-4).

Key limits: GST 2.0 revenue loss, petroleum/alcohol exclusion, State revenue stress.
AP angle: revenue-deficit State; 16th FC devolution and GST compensation end are decisive.
